parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A coil of insulated wire is wound on a copper core, as illustrated in Fig. 10.1.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

An alternating current is passed through the coil.

The heating effect of the current in the coil is negligible.

Explain why the temperature of the core rises.

markscheme_points.text: (non-uniform) magnetic flux in core is changing
induces (different) e.m.f. in (different parts of) the core

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what kind of magnetic field an alternating current in the coil creates inside the copper core.
Hint 2: Remember that copper is an electrical conductor even though it is a solid block, so ask yourself what Faraday's law says about a conductor in a changing flux.
Hint 3: Picture tiny closed loops inside the solid copper - what kind of currents could flow around those loops when different parts experience different induced e.m.f.?
Hint 4: Link those internal currents flowing through the resistance of copper to a thermal effect.
parts.proper_answer: The a.c. produces a continuously changing magnetic flux in the copper core. By Faraday's law this induces e.m.f.s in the conducting core. These drive eddy currents circulating in the core which dissipate power as heat in the resistance of the copper, raising its temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Changing Flux From The Coil**
Think of the coil as an electromagnet fed with a.c. The current keeps reversing, so the magnetic field it makes keeps reversing too. That means the magnetic flux inside the copper core is continuously changing in magnitude and direction.

Step 2: **Induction In The Core Itself**
Faraday's law tells us that any change of flux induces an e.m.f.: $$e = -\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}$$ The core is not just iron to guide flux, it is copper, a good conductor. So the changing flux induces e.m.f.s directly in the material of the core, with different values in different parts because the flux is non-uniform.

Step 3: **Eddy Currents Circulate**
Because copper conducts, those induced e.m.f.s drive real currents. There are no wires, so they flow in closed swirls inside the solid metal. We call these eddy currents. This is electromagnetic induction happening in bulk metal rather than in a neat coil.

Step 4: **Heating Raises The Temperature**
Copper has electrical resistance. Any current in a resistor dissipates thermal power by $P = I^2 R$. The eddy currents therefore heat the core from within, so its temperature rises even though the heating in the coil wire itself is negligible.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Two hollow tubes of equal length hang vertically as shown in Fig. 10.2.

{{figure:figure_10_2}}

One tube is made of plastic and the other of aluminium.

Two small similar bar magnets A and B are held above the tubes and then released simultaneously.

The magnets do not touch the sides of the tubes.
Explain why magnet B takes much longer than magnet A to fall through the tube.

markscheme_points.text: as magnet falls, tube cuts magnetic flux
with energy taken from falling magnet
so magnet B has acceleration < g or magnet B has smaller acceleration/reaches terminal speed

hints: Hint 1: Compare the two tubes as materials - which one can carry a current and which one is an insulator?
Hint 2: Think about what the falling magnet presents to the tube below and above it in terms of changing magnetic flux.
Hint 3: Apply Faraday's and Lenz's ideas to the conducting tube - what is induced there and what must the energy for any heating come from?
Hint 4: Consider what magnetic effect the induced currents themselves must produce and which way it acts on the falling magnet.
Hint 5: Link that opposing effect to the resultant acceleration compared to free fall at $g$ for magnet A in plastic.
parts.proper_answer: As magnet B falls the aluminium tube cuts its magnetic flux, inducing e.m.f. and eddy currents in the aluminium. The currents heat the tube, with energy taken from the gravitational potential energy of the falling magnet. By Lenz's law the eddy currents produce a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet, giving a retarding force. Hence acceleration of B is less than $g$ and B takes much longer to fall than A in the insulating plastic tube where no eddy currents form.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Only The Metal Tube Can Respond**
Magnet A falls through plastic, an insulator. No currents can be induced there, so A simply falls with acceleration $g$. Magnet B falls through aluminium, a conductor. Keep your eye on B, because only a conductor can have induced currents.

Step 2: **Falling Magnet Means Changing Flux**
As B moves down, the magnetic flux through each part of the aluminium wall is changing rapidly - increasing as the magnet approaches and decreasing as it passes. The tube is effectively cutting flux. By Faraday's law, $$e = -\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}$$ an e.m.f. is induced in the metal wall.

Step 3: **Eddy Currents And Energy Loss**
The induced e.m.f. drives eddy currents swirling around the aluminium tube. These currents heat the tube by $I^2R$ heating. Energy must be conserved, so this thermal energy can only come from the mechanical energy of the falling magnet. The magnet loses gravitational potential energy faster than it gains kinetic energy.

Step 4: **Lenz's Law Gives Braking**
Lenz's law says induced effects oppose the change causing them. The eddy currents create their own magnetic field with polarity that repels the approaching magnet below and attracts the receding magnet above. In both cases the force on the magnet is upward, opposite to its motion. It is magnetic braking with no contact.

Step 5: **Slower Fall For Magnet B**
For B the resultant downward force is weight minus upward magnetic drag, so resultant acceleration is less than $g$. It may even reach a low terminal speed. Magnet A has no drag and accelerates at $g$. That is why B takes much longer to pass through the same length of tube.
